summary.text: Carbon dioxide, CO₂, is a compound whose molecules each hold one carbon atom double bonded to two oxygen atoms, and it is a gas at room temperature.
In the air it lets visible light pass but absorbs infrared radiation, which makes it a greenhouse gas.
Its level in the atmosphere has climbed from 280 ppm before industry to 428 ppm, mainly from burning fossil fuels, and this rise is the primary cause of climate change.

facts.label: Taken up by sinks
facts.value: About half of excess emissions, by land and ocean

items.prompt: A beam holding both visible light and infrared radiation shines through air rich in carbon dioxide. What does the gas do to the beam?

options.label: Absorbs the visible part, lets infrared through
Lets the visible part through, absorbs infrared
Absorbs both parts, so the air looks dark
Lets both parts pass through untouched

items.explain: Carbon dioxide is transparent to visible light but absorbs infrared radiation, which is why it acts as a greenhouse gas.

items.prompt: The amount of carbon dioxide in the air has risen well above its pre-industrial level. What is the main cause?

options.label: More volcanic eruptions
Oceans warming and giving off gas
Burning coal, oil and gas
A growing human population breathing

items.explain: Burning fossil fuels is the main cause of the increased concentrations, which in turn are the primary cause of climate change.

items.prompt: One forest burns down in a wildfire; another, flattened by a storm, slowly rots. Which of the two returns carbon dioxide to the air?

options.label: Only the burning forest
Only the rotting forest
Neither, since trees lock carbon away for good
Both the burning and the rotting forest

items.explain: Carbon dioxide is released from organic material both when it decays and when it combusts, as in forest fires.

items.prompt: Over decades, more carbon dioxide from the air dissolves into seawater. How does this change the sea?

options.label: The sea becomes more acidic
The sea becomes much saltier
The sea becomes more alkaline
The sea loses its dissolved carbon

items.explain: Dissolved carbon dioxide forms carbonate and mainly bicarbonate, which causes ocean acidification as atmospheric levels rise.

items.prompt: Each year people add extra carbon dioxide to the atmosphere. Roughly how much of that excess do land and ocean soak up?

options.label: Almost none of it
About half of it
Nearly all of it
About a tenth of it

items.explain: Land and ocean carbon sinks absorb about half of excess emissions, and they can become saturated.

items.prompt: Carbon dioxide is denser than dry air. What actually happens to it once it is released into the atmosphere?

options.label: It sinks and pools in a layer by the ground
It breaks apart within a few days
It lasts a long time and mixes all through the air
It rises and collects at the top of the sky

items.explain: Although it is 53% denser than dry air, carbon dioxide is long-lived and thoroughly mixes in the atmosphere.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Carbon dioxide, written CO₂, is a chemical compound. Each of its molecules holds a single carbon atom, with two oxygen atoms attached to it by covalent double bonds. At room temperature it is a gas, and at the amounts people usually meet it has no smell.

paragraphs.heading: A gas that traps heat
paragraphs.text: In the air, CO₂ lets visible light pass straight through but soaks up infrared radiation. That behaviour is what makes it a greenhouse gas. It is only a trace part of the atmosphere. Even though it is 53% denser than dry air, it stays aloft for a long time and mixes evenly through the whole atmosphere.

paragraphs.heading: A rising level
paragraphs.text: Before industry, the air held about 280 parts per million (ppm) of CO₂, roughly 0.028%. By July 2025 that had reached 428 ppm, about 0.043%. The burning of fossil fuels is the main reason for the climb, and the climb in turn is the chief cause of climate change. Nearly all the CO₂ that people produce ends up in the atmosphere.

paragraphs.heading: The gas of life
paragraphs.text: Atmospheric CO₂ is the main source of carbon for living things on Earth. Plants, algae and cyanobacteria use the energy of sunlight to build carbohydrates out of CO₂ and water, a process called photosynthesis that gives off oxygen as waste. Aerobic organisms run the other way: to get energy from organic compounds by respiration, they use up oxygen and release CO₂. Rotting and burning, as in forest fires, also send it back to the air. Before industry, living things together with geological features kept its level regulated.

paragraphs.heading: Where the extra goes
paragraphs.text: Carbon sinks on land and in the ocean take up about half of the extra CO₂ that is emitted. These sinks can fill up, and they are unstable, since decay and wildfires can release the gas again. Over long spans, the carbon gets locked away in rocks and in deposits such as coal, petroleum and natural gas. CO₂ also dissolves in water, where it forms carbonate and mostly bicarbonate; as levels in the air go up, this makes the oceans more acidic, which is called ocean acidification.

paragraphs.heading: Put to work
paragraphs.text: Only a sliver of the CO₂ made each year, under 1%, is used commercially. Most of that goes into making fertilizer, and into the oil and gas industry for a method called enhanced oil recovery. Smaller uses include making food and drinks, working metal, cooling, putting out fires, and helping plants grow in greenhouses.
